name: Jade Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What do you do on a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I operate a rubber-gasket extrusion line. The rubber comes out as a long strip, and I measure the thickness before it is cut into seals for pumps. I am 58 and new to this line after years in a shop storeroom, so I still call the experienced operator when the strip curls. I left school after secondary education and receive the usual operator wage, not a lead rate.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How is home life, and how do you handle technology?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Nina does home-care visits, and our two children have their own households. We have about four months of expenses saved and a mortgage with some years left. There are a few other plants close enough for me to consider, but I would need an actual opening. I use AI now and then to put a long material sheet into ordinary words, then check with the senior operator. I can learn a new screen after seeing it work, but I do not want an untested setting on a production run. We discuss retirement, though we have not settled what income would cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the extrusion crew that quicker paperwork does not change the seal thickness we must measure. I would keep the gauge beside the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We can cover the mortgage with our present wages, and four months saved gives us a little room. I am still learning the rubber line, so I value a steady shift and the senior operator’s checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep measuring the first strip after each material change and ask before resetting the heater. I would sometimes use AI to understand a material note, then compare it with the printed specification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly calm about the machine work continuing. A slow AI change is manageable while the pay and checks stay in place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What shows that the gasket strip is wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The outside edge curls before the thickness gauge reaches the limit. A curled rubber edge can leak even when the strip measures the right width. I put a sample aside for the senior operator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an AI course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not just to repeat what I do on my phone. I would consider paid instruction if the plant introduced a new work screen. First I would need to see a reliable example on our own material.

say: I would **keep** gauge checks even if order paperwork becomes faster.
The **senior** operator should review uncertain rubber settings.
think: **Present** wages cover the mortgage and four months saved gives some room.
I **am** still learning this extrusion line.
do: **Keep** measuring first rubber strips after material changes.
**Verify** occasional AI explanations against printed specifications and senior advice.
feel: **Fairly** calm about a steady shift and familiar physical checks.
S0.quote: A curled rubber edge can leak even when the strip measures the right width.
fieldNote: **Jade** is a junior gasket-line operator who relies on a gauge and experienced colleague.
Her **partner** Nina works in home care; their grown children live independently and the household has a mortgage.
**Four** months saved, typical operator pay and a few nearby plants make the quiet picture manageable.

steps.text: Keep measuring first gasket strips and checking uncertain settings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew office software may change orders before robots touch the rubber line. I would ask the union branch for the proposed staffing numbers before any feeder is installed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot feeder could remove a helper and later leave fewer shifts for someone still junior like me. Four months saved would buy time but not restore a cut wage. Nina’s care visits have variable hours, so I would want exact figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to watch a guarded feeder trial and compare its damaged seals with our current batch record. I would attend the union meeting on staffing and paid safety training. If the plant posts a gasket-checking role, I would apply only if the wage and hours cover our mortgage and Nina’s care rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my place on the roster. I can learn from watching a robot run, but watching does not prove I can operate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you volunteer to operate the feeder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after an offered funded paid training place with supervised guards, stops and isolation practice. I would need to pass the check with a trainer beside me. A demonstration alone is not a qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no checking role is posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current wage and look at posted operator jobs at the other local plants. I would compare their pay, travel and shift times with the mortgage before applying. A supposed vacancy is not enough.

**Office** order software arrives before robot feeding.
think: A **later** robot feeder may cut my junior gasket-line shifts.
**Four** months saved cannot replace a lasting wage cut.
do: **Request** guarded feeder trial and compare damaged seals.
**Attend** union branch meeting about staffing and safety.
**Apply** for posted gasket-checking role only with mortgage-covering pay and workable hours.
feel: **Anxious** about roster risk, careful not to confuse observation with skill.
S1.quote: I can learn from watching a robot run, but watching does not prove I can operate it.
fieldNote: **Jade** requests an observed trial and would operate only after an offered funded paid supervised safety place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the branch AGI can handle orders in 2028, while capable robots feeding, inspecting and clearing the gasket line arrive around 2031. We need written wage and redeployment terms before the second change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect our line to need far fewer operators after the robot can handle a whole run. I will be 63 then, still a junior on this machine. Four months saved will go quickly if my wage falls while Nina’s care hours also fluctuate, and I would lie awake about the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would postpone the planned roof work and list the bills that cannot wait. I would ask the union branch to seek written redeployment terms and ask our lender about payment options before any missed instalment. I would apply for a posted local inspection job only with paid supervised safety instruction, a net wage that covers our bills and shifts compatible with home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed at the expected loss of this shift. Having four months saved gives a start, but it is not a second wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you move straight into inspection?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know a gauge, not a robot cell. I would need an actual paid supervised place to learn safe isolation before accepting those duties. A job posting must also tell me what the wage is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children help with the roof?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own bills. If one offers help, I would thank them, but I would not put the mortgage on their shoulders. We would delay the roof work and use written lender terms instead.

say: I would **seek** written terms before robots reach the gasket line around 2031.
think: **Four** months saved and variable household hours make the mortgage vulnerable.
do: **Postpone** planned roof work and list essential bills.
**Ask** union for redeployment terms and lender for payment options.
**Apply** for posted inspection work only with paid safe training bill-covering net wage and workable shifts.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected shift loss and awake worrying over mortgage payments.
S2.quote: I know a gauge, not a robot cell.
fieldNote: **Jade** expects physical line displacement around 2031, about three years after AGI changes ordering.
Her **four-month** buffer cannot sustain a long cut to her typical wage alongside variable care-work hours.
**Inspection** requires an actual posting, paid supervised safety training, adequate net pay and workable shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the plant five years is time to offer paid practical places, including to the junior operators. AGI changes orders in 2031 and capable hands-on robots reach the gasket line around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 66 near the robot date. I have learned the rubber line late, and a robot arm is another step. Retirement is in sight, but I cannot assume our income will cover the mortgage without seeing the figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would enrol in a recognised quality-and-robot-safety course only if offered a funded paid place with supervised isolation practice and class times that fit my work hours. After completing it, I would apply for a posted local inspection role only if its net pay, travel and shifts cover our bills. If no paid course opens, I would keep the line wage and check posted local gasket jobs with sufficient pay and workable hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about spending training time without a later place. I can learn after others prove a method, but I need a wage while doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your diploma help with the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have secondary school, not a technical diploma. I would start with basic machine diagrams and a trainer showing safe stops. The recognised course must teach me, not assume I already know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire rather than train?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nina and I would first get actual estimates and add our mortgage and living costs. I would not set my factory exit date from a birthday alone. If the figures do not work, I need paid employment.

**Robots** reach the line around 2034 after AGI changes orders.
think: At 66, **retirement** income is still uncertain while our mortgage remains.
I **need** real supervised robot safety instruction.
do: **Enrol** in offered recognised funded paid course with supervised isolation and workable class hours.
**Apply** after course for posted inspection work only with bill-covering net pay travel and shifts.
If **no** paid course, seek posted gasket work with sufficient wage and hours.
feel: **Anxious** about a real course place and later paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the union branch a ten-year warning should come with paid courses and transparent retirement figures. AGI changes orders in 2036, while capable robots reach the line around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 68 in 2036 and 71 when robots arrive. I may have stopped full shifts by then, but we have not priced that choice. If I still need a wage, a long runway helps only with an offered place and an actual job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request written household retirement income and cost estimates. If they show I still need to work, I would take an offered recognised funded paid course with supervised robot isolation on attendable hours, then apply for a posted local inspection job only if its net pay and shifts cover our bills. Without that paid place I would check posted gasket jobs with adequate wages and hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about unknown income after work. Time lets Nina and me calculate; it does not guarantee a safe course or a retirement payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask at the union meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the branch to push for paid older-worker course places and written training criteria. A public promise is useful only when operators can see who qualifies. I would take that question to an actual meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep working if retirement figures cover the bills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might choose to stop full shifts once the estimates are firm and the mortgage is covered. I would not claim that money now. The 2039 robot date may come after my last factory shift.

I would **distinguish** 2036 orders from 2039 robot work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most because a robot could cut my gasket-line shifts around 2031, before our four months saved carries us very far. Funded paid safety instruction and a posted job with enough net pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I am willing to try a good screen when another operator can show it works on our rubber. A curled rubber edge can leak even when the strip measures the right width.

headlineQuote: I am willing to try a good screen when another operator can show it works on our rubber.
portrait: **Jade** Garcia, 58, is a junior rubber-gasket machine operator with secondary schooling and typical pay.
She and **home-care** partner Nina have grown children, a mortgage and about four months of expenses saved.
She **uses** AI occasionally for material sheets, verifies printed specifications and adopts proven technology after others.
She **favours** union action and paid safe training, while a possible loss of junior hours makes her anxious.
**Retirement** is conditional on real income figures; posted work needs sufficient net pay, travel and workable shifts.
biggestWorry: **Capable** robots around 2031 could cut her gasket-line hours before the household can build more reserves.
whatWouldHelp: **Offer** recognised funded paid supervised training and posted jobs with bill-covering net wages and workable hours.
